title: Raising Chickens for Eggs and Meat
summary: Set up a small backyard flock that keeps laying when stores are empty: breeds, coop space, predator-proofing, feed and water, and safe egg handling based on university extension guidance.

steps.title: Check local rules and plan flock size
steps.body: Before you buy birds, check your city or county code and any HOA rules. Many towns cap backyard flocks at a handful of hens, ban roosters, and require the coop to sit behind the house and a set distance from property lines and neighbors. Some states also require poultry registration. Plan on roughly one egg per hen about every 25 hours during good laying months, and much less in winter and during molt. A household of four that wants an egg a day each needs about six to eight hens. Start small. Three to six birds teach you the routine without overwhelming your feed budget or your yard.

steps.title: Pick hardy dual-purpose breeds
steps.body: For self-reliance, choose heritage dual-purpose breeds that lay well and dress out to a usable carcass. Common choices are Rhode Island Red, Barred Plymouth Rock, Sussex, Orpington, and Australorp. They are calm, cold-hardy, and decent foragers. Leghorns lay more eggs but are small and flighty, so they give little meat. Cornish Cross broilers grow to butcher weight in about two months but are not layers and do poorly free-ranging. Buy from a hatchery or breeder that takes part in the National Poultry Improvement Plan, which tests for key diseases. Keep new adult birds apart from your flock for about 30 days before mixing.

steps.title: Give each bird enough coop and run space
steps.body: Crowding causes pecking, disease, and stress. University of Tennessee Extension guidance calls for about 3 square feet (0.3 sq m) of coop floor per light-breed bird and 4 square feet (0.4 sq m) per heavy breed, plus 8 to 10 square feet (0.7 to 0.9 sq m) each of outdoor run. Provide 8 to 9 inches (20 to 23 cm) of roost bar per bird, with bars 12 to 14 inches (30 to 36 cm) apart. Add one 12 by 12 inch (30 by 30 cm) nest box for every four to five hens, placed in a dim, quiet spot. Vent the coop high under the roof so ammonia and moisture escape without a draft blowing across the roost.

steps.title: Predator-proof with hardware cloth and nightly lockup
steps.body: Predators are the biggest flock killer. University of Maryland Extension advises covering every opening with 1/4 or 1/2 inch (6 or 13 mm) galvanized hardware cloth, not chicken wire, which raccoons tear through and which rusts. Bury hardware cloth 12 to 18 inches (30 to 45 cm) deep around the coop, or bend fence mesh outward along the ground so diggers hit wire. Raise the coop at least 1 foot (30 cm) off the ground. Lock birds in every night, because most losses happen after dark. Cover the run top if hawks hunt your area. Hawks and owls are federally protected, so you may not trap or shoot them: use netting and cover instead.

steps.title: Feed and water every day
steps.body: A laying hen eats about 1/4 to 1/3 pound (110 to 140 g) of feed per day. A complete commercial layer ration is the simplest way to keep production up. Offer crushed oyster shell on the side so hens can take extra calcium for strong shells. Kitchen scraps and garden waste can stretch feed, but keep them a small share of the diet, and never feed moldy or spoiled food. Stockpile at least a month of feed in sealed metal cans to beat rodents and moisture. Water needs climb with heat: about 8 to 10 ounces (240 to 300 ml) per bird per day in cool weather and up to 16 ounces (470 ml) above 90°F (32°C). In winter, change frozen water at least twice a day or use a heated base.

steps.title: Collect and handle eggs safely
steps.body: Collect eggs at least once a day, and twice is better, because each hen visit can soil the nest. Keep nests clean with fresh bedding. Set dirty and floor eggs apart from clean ones. Alabama Extension advises dry-cleaning lightly soiled eggs with a clean cloth or fine sandpaper. If you must wash, use running water at least 20°F (11°C) warmer than the egg, never soak eggs, and dry them fully. Washing removes the natural bloom, so refrigerate washed eggs. Discard very dirty or cracked eggs rather than eating them. Store eggs at 33 to 40°F (1 to 4°C) when you can, and cook them until yolk and white are firm.

steps.title: Protect your household from Salmonella
steps.body: Healthy-looking chickens can carry Salmonella on feathers, feet, and in droppings. Wash hands with soap and water right after touching birds, eggs, feeders, or anything in the coop. Keep coop boots and clothes outside the house. Do not let birds into the kitchen, and do not kiss or snuggle them. Children under 5, adults over 65, and anyone with a weak immune system should be supervised closely or skip handling. Clean feeders and waterers regularly so birds do not pass germs to each other. If birds suddenly die, stop laying, or show swollen heads or breathing trouble, isolate them and contact your state veterinarian or extension office, since avian influenza must be reported.

warnings: Chicken wire keeps chickens in but does not keep predators out. Use hardware cloth on every opening.
Salmonella spreads from birds and coop surfaces to people. Wash hands every time, and keep young children from handling birds unsupervised.
Sudden deaths or many sick birds can mean avian influenza. Do not eat or sell those birds or eggs, and report it to your state veterinarian.
Never feed moldy grain or spoiled scraps. Mold toxins can sicken or kill a flock.
proTips: Put the coop where you can see it from a window. You will notice predator trouble and sick birds sooner.
Keep a deep layer of dry litter (pine shavings or straw) and turn it often. Spent litter makes excellent compost.
Mark the hatch month on each bird's leg band so you know which hens are aging out of good production.
Hens slow down or stop laying when daylight drops below about 14 hours. Expect fewer winter eggs and store extras from spring.
source: University of Maryland, Tennessee, and Alabama Extension

sources.title: Enhancing Egg Quality and Safety in Small Flocks

whenNotTo: Your local ordinance or lease bans poultry - fines and forced removal waste your investment.
You cannot lock the birds in every night or check them daily.
Someone in the household is at high risk from Salmonella and cannot avoid contact with the birds.

quickGlance.situation: You want a reliable, renewable supply of eggs and some meat from a small backyard flock.
immediate: Check local poultry rules before buying birds.
Build or buy a coop with hardware cloth on every opening.
Start with 3 to 6 hardy dual-purpose hens.
then: Lock birds in every night and collect eggs daily.
Wash hands after every contact with birds, eggs, or the coop.

title: Emergency Gardening - High-Yield Crops for Food Security
summary: Plan and plant a vegetable garden that produces as much food as possible, as early as possible, using frost dates, crop timing, and succession planting from extension guidance.

steps.title: Pick the sunniest, best-drained spot
steps.body: Vegetables need sun. Put the garden away from trees and buildings that cast shade, and close to the house, water, and tools so you actually tend it. Most fruiting crops such as tomatoes, peppers, beans, and squash need at least 6 hours of direct sun. Leafy greens tolerate partial shade. Choose ground that drains after rain. Avoid low spots that puddle, areas near old buildings with flaking lead paint, and spots near treated lumber or fuel spills. If you can, send a soil sample to your state's extension soil-testing lab. The test tells you the pH and which nutrients to add, so you do not waste scarce fertilizer.

steps.title: Find your frost dates and work backward
steps.body: Your average last spring frost and first fall frost set the whole calendar. Get them from your county extension office or a nearby weather station. University of Delaware Extension sets tender crops like tomatoes and peppers out about 2 weeks after the date when frost risk falls to about 10 percent. For any crop, count back from the first fall frost using the days to maturity on the seed packet, and add about 2 weeks of buffer. If a crop needs 70 days and you only have 50 frost-free days left, plant something faster. Write the dates on a simple calendar so you do not miss planting windows.

steps.title: Plant fast crops first for early food
steps.body: While long-season crops grow, fast crops feed you. Radishes can be ready in about 25 to 30 days. Leaf lettuce, arugula, and spinach give cuttings in about 30 to 50 days. Bush beans produce in about 50 to 60 days. Turnips and their greens are ready in about 45 to 60 days, and the greens can be cut sooner. These cool-season crops (spinach, lettuce, radish, peas, kale, cabbage) go in early spring and again in late summer for fall. Warm-season crops (beans, squash, tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers) wait until the soil warms and frost has passed. Mixing both groups gives you something to eat most of the season.

steps.title: Grow calorie crops, not just salad
steps.body: Greens are nutritious but have very few calories. To actually feed a family, give real space to energy-dense crops. Potatoes and sweet potatoes produce a lot of calories per square foot and store well. Winter squash and pumpkins store for months. Dry beans supply protein and keep for years once dried. Corn, if you have room for a block of at least four rows for pollination, gives grain for meal. Onions and garlic store well and add flavor. A good emergency plan pairs a few calorie crops with fast greens for vitamins. Choose open-pollinated varieties of these crops if you plan to save seed.

steps.title: Build beds without heavy digging
steps.body: If you are starting on lawn, sheet mulching saves labor. Mow the grass short, cover it with overlapping plain cardboard, wet it well, and pile 4 to 6 inches (10 to 15 cm) of compost, leaves, or straw on top. Plant transplants into pockets of compost. The grass dies and rots under the cardboard over a season. Raised beds about 4 feet (1.2 m) wide let you reach the middle without stepping on the soil. Keep walking paths separate so planting areas stay loose. Use untreated wood or stone for edging around food crops if you can.

steps.title: Use succession and intensive planting
steps.body: Succession planting means sowing the same crop on several dates, so harvests come in waves instead of all at once. University of Delaware Extension gives the example of three sweet corn plantings from early May to early July. Replant each bed as soon as you clear it: follow spring peas with beans, and follow early potatoes with fall greens. Tuck quick crops such as radishes between slow ones like tomatoes. Spreading harvests over 7 to 8 months means you eat more fresh and have less to preserve at one time. Keep a notebook of what you planted, when, and how it did. It is the best tool for next year.

steps.title: Water, mulch, and scout for pests
steps.body: Most gardens need about 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water per week from rain or irrigation. Water deeply at the base of plants in the morning rather than sprinkling leaves at night, which spreads disease. Mulch with straw, leaves, or grass clippings to hold moisture and smother weeds. Walk the garden every day or two and look under leaves for eggs, beetles, and caterpillars. Hand-pick pests into soapy water. Pull diseased plants and do not compost them in a cool pile. Rotate crop families to new beds each year so soil pests and diseases do not build up.

warnings: Do not grow food in soil near old painted buildings, roads, or fuel spills without a soil test - lead and other contaminants can be taken up or splashed onto crops.
Read every pesticide label, even organic ones, and follow the waiting period before harvest.
A garden takes weeks to months to produce. It supplements stored food; it does not replace it in the first weeks of an emergency.
proTips: Start tomato, pepper, and cabbage seedlings indoors 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost to gain weeks of harvest.
Keep a two-year supply of seed in a cool, dry, sealed container so one bad season does not end your garden.
Your county extension office and Master Gardener volunteers can tell you which varieties do best in your area - usually for free.
source: University of Delaware / Penn State / UMass Extension

sources.title: Container Vegetable Gardening: Four Keys to Success

whenNotTo: You need food in the next few days - eat from stored food first and plant for the weeks ahead.
The only available ground is contaminated (flood silt, chemical spills, old lead-paint areas) - use containers with fresh potting mix instead.

quickGlance.situation: You need to start growing as much food as possible from a backyard or small plot.
immediate: Find your last and first frost dates.
Plant fast greens and radishes now if the season allows.
Set aside the sunniest space for potatoes, squash, and beans.
then: Replant each bed as soon as you harvest it.
Mulch, water deeply, and check for pests every day or two.

title: Preserving Food Without Electricity
summary: An overview of safe ways to keep a harvest without a freezer - canning, fermenting, drying, curing, and cold storage - with the tested rules that prevent botulism and food poisoning.

steps.title: Match the method to the food
steps.body: Each preservation method works by stopping germs in a different way: heat (canning), acid (fermenting and pickling), removing water (drying), salt and nitrite (curing), or cold (root cellars). Not every method is safe for every food. Low-acid foods such as vegetables, meat, poultry, and fish must be pressure canned, never boiled in a water bath. Fruits, acidified tomatoes, pickles, and sauerkraut can be water-bath canned using a tested recipe. Root crops and winter squash keep for months in cool storage with no processing at all. Choose the simplest safe method for each crop before you harvest, and gather the gear and supplies ahead of time.

steps.title: Use only tested recipes
steps.body: The USDA, the National Center for Home Food Preservation (NCHFP), and university extension services publish recipes that were lab-tested for heat penetration and acidity. Follow them exactly. Do not add extra onions, peppers, or thickeners, change jar sizes, or shorten times, because those changes can leave the center of a jar under-processed. Recipes from old cookbooks, social media, or family tradition are often unsafe. Writers frequently promote methods the USDA does not support, such as oven canning, open-kettle canning, and canning in electric multicookers. Print the tested recipes you will need and keep them with your canning gear in case the internet is down.

steps.title: Understand the botulism risk
steps.body: Clostridium botulinum spores are in soil everywhere and survive boiling water at 212°F (100°C). In a sealed jar of low-acid food with no oxygen, they can grow and make a toxin that paralyzes nerves and can stop breathing. The CDC says contaminated food may look, smell, and taste normal. That is why the rules matter: pressure canning reaches about 240°F (116°C), which kills the spores, and acid at a pH of 4.6 or lower stops them from growing. Throw out any jar that is leaking, bulging, cracked, spurting, foaming, moldy, or smells off. Never taste food to check it. Anyone with blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, or trouble swallowing after eating home-preserved food needs emergency care immediately.

steps.title: Ferment vegetables with measured salt
steps.body: Fermentation lets lactic acid bacteria sour the food. The NCHFP sauerkraut recipe uses about 3 tablespoons of canning or pickling salt per 5 pounds (2.3 kg) of shredded cabbage. Pack it firmly so the juice covers the cabbage. If it does not, add brine made from 1 1/2 tablespoons of salt per quart (1 liter) of water. Keep the cabbage under the brine with a plate and weight or a brine-filled food-grade bag. At 70 to 75°F (21 to 24°C), it ferments in about 3 to 4 weeks. At 60 to 65°F (16 to 18°C) it takes 5 to 6 weeks. Below 60°F it may not ferment, and above 75°F it can turn soft. Throw out kraut that is slimy, pink, or moldy beyond surface scum.

steps.title: Dry foods until brittle or leathery
steps.body: Drying removes the water germs need. Fruits and vegetables can be sun-dried in hot, dry climates or dried in a low oven or dehydrator. Dry fruit until leathery with no pockets of moisture and vegetables until brittle. Condition dried fruit by packing it loosely in a jar for a week and shaking daily. If droplets form, dry it longer. Meat is different: USDA FSIS advises heating meat to 160°F (71°C), or poultry to 165°F (74°C), before or during drying, because drying temperatures alone may not kill bacteria. Store dried foods in airtight containers in a cool, dark place. Home-dried jerky keeps about 1 to 2 months.

steps.title: Cure meat only with a tested cure
steps.body: Salt curing is old, but it is not foolproof. Mississippi State Extension recommends a commercial cure that contains measured sodium nitrite, used at the recipe's rate per pound and kept at 32 to 40°F (0 to 4°C) during curing. Nitrite helps stop botulism in cured meats, but too much is toxic, so never guess the amount. Dry curing takes about 7 days per inch (2.5 cm) of thickness. Hams cured for a shorter time are not shelf stable and must be frozen or refrigerated. Aging hams at room temperature is risky in warm, humid climates. Beginners should cure in cold weather, follow one tested recipe closely, and cook cured products fully unless the recipe is a tested dry-cured one.

steps.title: Store and rotate what you preserve
steps.body: Label every jar and bag with the food, the method, and the date. Store canned goods in a cool, dry, dark place. Home-canned food keeps its best quality for about one year, so eat the oldest first. Check stored jars before use for broken seals. Keep fermented foods cold once they finish, ideally below 40°F (4°C). Check root-cellar produce weekly and remove anything rotting before it spreads. Keep a simple inventory sheet so you know what you have and can plan meals instead of letting food age past its best quality.

warnings: Never water-bath can vegetables, meat, poultry, fish, or beans. Only a pressure canner kills botulism spores in low-acid foods.
Botulism toxin often gives no sign. Food can look and smell normal. If a jar's processing is in doubt, throw it out without tasting.
Curing salts with nitrite are toxic in excess. Measure exactly, keep them labeled, and store them away from table salt and children.
Botulism symptoms (double or blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing or breathing) are a medical emergency. Call 911 or get to a hospital.
proTips: Buy bottled lemon juice for canning tomatoes. Its acidity is consistent, unlike fresh lemons.
Ferment in a cool basement in late summer to hit the ideal 60 to 75°F range without power.
Root cellaring and drying need no special fuel. Save canning, which needs a steady heat source, for foods that cannot be stored any other way.
source: USDA / NCHFP / CDC / USDA FSIS / MSU Extension

sources.title: Sauerkraut
sources.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation

whenNotTo: You do not have a tested recipe for that food and method - store it another way or eat it fresh.
You cannot hold the needed temperature (steady canner pressure, a cool curing space, or a 60 to 75°F fermenting spot).
The food is already spoiling - preservation does not make bad food safe.

quickGlance.situation: You have more food than you can eat fresh and no refrigeration or freezer.
immediate: Put root crops, squash, and onions in cool storage first - no processing needed.
Pressure can low-acid foods; water-bath only high-acid or acidified foods.
Use only USDA, NCHFP, or extension tested recipes.
then: Label and date everything and eat the oldest first.
Throw out any bulging, leaking, or off-smelling jar without tasting it.

title: Water Collection and Storage for a Homestead
summary: Collect, store, and treat rainwater for a homestead: barrels and tanks, first-flush diverters, what roof water is safe for, and how to disinfect it before drinking using EPA guidance.

steps.title: Work out how much water you need
steps.body: Plan at least 1 gallon (3.8 liters) per person per day for drinking and basic food prep, and more in hot weather or for nursing mothers, children, and sick people. Washing, cooking, and sanitation push real household use far higher. Animals add more: a laying hen drinks up to about a pint (0.5 liters) a day in heat, and goats and garden beds need much more. Add up people, animals, and garden, then multiply by the longest dry spell you expect. That number tells you whether a few barrels will do or you need large tanks. Check state law first. A few Western states limit rainwater capture.

steps.title: Size your catchment
steps.body: Roofs collect a surprising amount. A useful rule: each inch (2.5 cm) of rain on 1,000 square feet (93 sq m) of roof yields about 600 gallons (2,270 liters), minus losses for splash and first flush. Measure the footprint of the roof that drains to each downspout, not the sloped surface. Then compare that to your storage. A single 55-gallon (208-liter) barrel fills from less than a tenth of an inch of rain on an average roof, so many homesteads link several barrels or step up to 275 or 330 gallon (1,000 to 1,250 liter) food-grade IBC totes or a cistern.

steps.title: Set up barrels with screens and a first-flush diverter
steps.body: Use only food-grade containers that never held chemicals. Put a fine screen on every inlet and overflow to keep out leaves, mosquitoes, and rodents. Install a first-flush diverter at the downspout. It catches the first gallons of each rain, which carry the most bird droppings, dust, and roof grit, and sends cleaner water to the barrel. Set barrels on a level, solid base: a full 55-gallon barrel weighs more than 450 pounds (200 kg). Raise them on blocks so you get gravity pressure at the spigot. Route overflow away from your foundation and your neighbor's yard.

steps.title: Know what roof water is safe for
steps.body: Untreated roof water is fine for most garden and livestock uses, but it is not safe to drink as-is. It can carry bacteria from bird and animal droppings, and metals or chemicals from roofing, flashing, and gutters. Asphalt shingles, treated wood shakes, and old lead flashing or paint add contaminants. Metal roofs with food-safe coatings give the cleanest water. Water vegetable soil, not leaves, and wash produce well. Use the cleanest water you have for drinking, and treat it every time.

steps.title: Treat water before you drink it
steps.body: If water is cloudy, let it settle, then pour it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter. Then disinfect. EPA says boiling is the best method: bring water to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 5,000 feet (1,000 m). To use unscented household bleach, check the label strength. For 6 percent bleach, add 8 drops per gallon. For 8.25 percent bleach, add 6 drops per gallon. Double the dose if the water is cloudy, colored, or very cold. Stir and wait 30 minutes. It should smell slightly of chlorine. If not, repeat the dose and wait 15 more minutes. Disinfection does not remove chemicals, fuel, or metals.

steps.title: Store treated water correctly
steps.body: Keep drinking water in clean, food-grade containers with tight lids, out of sunlight, and away from fuel, pesticides, and chemicals. Sunlight grows algae in clear or light-colored containers. Label each container with the date it was filled and treated. Rotate stored tap or treated water about every 6 months. Use a clean scoop or spigot, never your hands or a dirty cup, to draw water. Keep separate, clearly marked containers for non-drinking water so no one mixes them up.

steps.title: Maintain the system every season
steps.body: Clean gutters at least twice a year and after storms. Empty and clean the first-flush diverter after each big rain or as its design requires. Once a year, drain each barrel, scrub it with a mild bleach solution, and rinse well. Check screens monthly for holes, because a gap can let mosquitoes breed in your barrel within days. In freezing climates, drain and disconnect barrels before hard frost or they can split. Watch for leaks, algae, and smells, and fix problems before you depend on the water.

warnings: Do not drink untreated rainwater. Boil or disinfect it every time.
Bleach and boiling kill germs but do not remove fuel, chemicals, or heavy metals. Do not drink water that may be chemically contaminated.
Never use containers that held chemicals, fuel, or pesticides, even after washing.
Cover and screen every barrel. Open water grows mosquitoes and can drown small children and animals.
proTips: Mark the downspout and barrel used for drinking-grade collection and keep it to the cleanest section of roof.
Paint or wrap translucent tanks dark, or keep them in shade, to stop algae.
Link barrels at the bottom with short hoses so they fill and drain together from one spigot.
source: U.S. EPA / Lake Champlain Sea Grant

sources.title: Rain Barrel Water Reuse: Summary of Research and Recommendations
sources.publisher: Lake Champlain Sea Grant / University of Vermont

whenNotTo: Your state restricts rainwater capture - check the law before building a large system.
The roof or gutters are contaminated by smoke, ash, chemicals, or lead paint - do not use that water for drinking even after treatment.

quickGlance.situation: You need a steady water supply for your household, animals, and garden without city water.
immediate: Calculate household, animal, and garden water needs.
Install food-grade barrels with screens and a first-flush diverter.
Boil or bleach-treat any rainwater before drinking.
then: Store treated water sealed, labeled, and out of sunlight.
Clean gutters, diverters, and barrels on a regular schedule.

title: Home Slaughter and Processing Basics
summary: Process your own poultry and small livestock humanely and cleanly: legal limits, preparation, scalding and evisceration, rapid chilling to 40°F, and which carcasses to throw away, based on university extension guidance.

steps.title: Know the legal limits first
steps.body: In the U.S., you may slaughter your own animals on your own property for your own household without inspection. Selling or trading that meat is a different matter. University of Illinois Extension notes that meat for sale must come from a licensed, inspected facility. Minnesota Extension explains a federal exemption that lets small producers sell up to 1,000 home-processed chickens, turkeys, or geese a year within their state, but uninspected poultry can never cross state lines, and states add their own rules. Call your state department of agriculture before selling anything. For cattle, hogs, and other large animals, a licensed custom processor is often the safest choice.

steps.title: Plan the day, the place, and the cold
steps.body: Illinois Extension advises slaughtering only when the air is below 40°F (4°C), or having enough ice and cold water to chill carcasses fast, because bacteria multiply quickly above 40°F. Work in the coolest part of the day with good light. Choose a clean, fly-free area with plenty of drinkable water. Use nonporous tables covered with disposable plastic. Have sharp knives, a sanitizing pot of boiling water, soap, a thermometer, coolers of ice water, and freezer space ready before you start. Plan on large amounts of meat: a 280-pound (127 kg) hog yields roughly 135 to 155 pounds (61 to 70 kg) of bone-in cuts.

steps.title: Prepare the animals and dispatch humanely
steps.body: Minnesota Extension advises withholding feed from poultry for 6 to 8 hours before slaughter while keeping water available. An empty gut is less likely to spill and contaminate meat. Keep birds in a clean holding cage with a wire floor. Animals should be made insensible to pain before slaughter by a quick, effective method. Follow the AVMA Guidelines for the Humane Slaughter of Animals for the right method for each species. For poultry, a restraining cone and a quick, deep cut with a very sharp knife is common. Get hands-on training from an experienced person first. A poorly done kill is cruel to the animal and dangerous to you.

steps.title: Bleed out, scald, and pluck poultry
steps.body: Let the bird bleed out fully in the cone, usually a minute or two. Then scald to loosen feathers. Minnesota Extension gives these scald targets: young chickens at 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) for 30 to 75 seconds, older chickens near 140°F (60°C) for 30 to 75 seconds, and ducks and geese at 160 to 170°F (71 to 77°C) for 1 to 2 minutes. Use a thermometer and keep hot water nearby to adjust. When wing and tail feathers pull out easily, pluck by hand or with a drum plucker. Finish killing and scalding all birds before you start eviscerating, so dirty work stays separate from clean work.

steps.title: Eviscerate without nicking the gut
steps.body: Cut carefully around the vent without puncturing the intestine. Pull the vent and organs out together so their contents never touch the body cavity. If feces, gut contents, or milk touch meat on any animal, trim that meat and fat away and discard it. Illinois Extension advises washing knives often, especially when moving from skin to inner tissue, and sanitizing them in boiling water. Wash hands and forearms between steps. Rinse carcasses with drinkable water from the top down. Illinois Extension also suggests a spray of 2.5 percent acetic acid (5 percent vinegar diluted half and half with water) after rinsing.

steps.title: Inspect organs and condemn sick carcasses
steps.body: Look at the organs and carcass for signs of disease. Minnesota Extension says to discard a bird with lumps or spots on the liver, any measurable fluid in the body cavity, organs twice normal size, orange fat on a thin bird, or abnormal streaks or swelling in the meat. Small defects like bruises, breast blisters, and skin tears can be trimmed and the rest used. For larger animals, any sign of disease on the head, organs, or carcass means the animal should not be eaten. Having a local veterinarian on site is strongly recommended for large livestock. When in doubt, throw it out.

steps.title: Chill fast, then package and freeze
steps.body: Get meat cold quickly. Pre-chill poultry in overflowing cold water, then hold it in ice water until the meat reaches 40°F (4°C). Small birds take a couple of hours and turkeys several hours. Drain about 10 minutes before bagging, and do not freeze birds until they are chilled to 40°F or below. Large carcasses take a long time to chill, so Illinois Extension favors cutting, packaging, and freezing promptly over long refrigerated holding. Keep everything cold, covered, and clean. Wrap meat airtight, label it with the date, and clean all tools and surfaces with soap and hot water when you finish.

warnings: Selling or trading uninspected meat is illegal in most cases. Check your state rules before offering any meat to others.
Do not eat any animal that was sick, died on its own, or shows abnormal organs.
Sharp knives and struggling animals cause serious cuts. Restrain animals properly, cut away from your body, and keep a first aid kit within reach.
Meat left above 40°F (4°C) grows bacteria fast. Do not slaughter on a warm day without enough ice to chill carcasses quickly.
proTips: Process a few birds at a time on your first day. Speed comes with practice; cleanliness should not be sacrificed for it.
Wait 1 to 2 weeks to process birds full of pin feathers. They are much harder to pluck.
Your extension office may offer hands-on poultry processing workshops. One supervised session teaches more than any guide.
source: University of Minnesota / University of Illinois Extension
whenNotTo: You cannot chill carcasses to 40°F quickly - wait for cold weather or arrange a processor.
The animal is sick or showed signs of disease before slaughter.
You have never done it and have no experienced person to train you on large livestock - use a licensed custom processor.

quickGlance.situation: You need to turn your own poultry or livestock into safe, clean meat at home.
immediate: Confirm local and state rules, especially if anyone else will eat or buy the meat.
Prepare ice water, sharp sanitized knives, and a clean work area before starting.
Withhold feed from poultry 6 to 8 hours beforehand.
then: Inspect organs and discard any carcass with signs of disease.
Chill meat to 40°F, then package and freeze promptly.

title: Home Canning Safely - Water-Bath vs. Pressure Canning
summary: Choose the right canning method, follow tested USDA and NCHFP recipes, adjust for altitude, and check seals so home-canned food never causes botulism.

steps.title: Sort foods by acidity
steps.body: The method depends on acid. Foods with a pH of 4.6 or lower are high-acid and can be canned in a boiling-water bath. These include most fruits, jams and jellies, pickles, sauerkraut, and tomatoes that have acid added. Foods with a pH above 4.6 are low-acid and must be pressure canned. These include all fresh vegetables, beans, meat, poultry, fish, seafood, soups, and mixes such as meat sauce. Boiling water reaches only 212°F (100°C), which does not kill botulism spores. A pressure canner reaches about 240°F (116°C), which does. There is no safe shortcut for low-acid foods.

steps.title: Use a tested recipe and the right equipment
steps.body: The CDC recommends following only the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or recipes tested by the National Center for Home Food Preservation and extension services. Do not change ingredient amounts, thicken with flour or cornstarch, or add extra onions, peppers, or mushrooms, since that can change acidity and heat penetration. Use mason jars, new flat lids, and bands. For pressure canning, use a true pressure canner big enough to hold at least four quart jars upright. The CDC says not to use electric multicookers or pressure cookers for canning, even if they have a canning button. Oven canning, open-kettle canning, and dishwasher canning are not safe.

steps.title: Acidify tomatoes in every jar
steps.body: Tomatoes sit near the pH line, so the NCHFP requires added acid even if you pressure can them. Add the acid to each jar before filling. Per quart, add 2 tablespoons of bottled lemon juice or 1/2 teaspoon of citric acid. Per pint, add 1 tablespoon of bottled lemon juice or 1/4 teaspoon of citric acid. Four tablespoons of 5 percent vinegar per quart also works but changes the flavor. You may add sugar to balance sourness, but never reduce the acid. Use bottled lemon juice, not fresh, because its acidity is standardized. Do not can tomatoes from dead or frost-killed vines.

steps.title: Water-bath can high-acid foods
steps.body: Prepare jars and fill them, leaving the headspace the recipe lists, usually 1/4 to 1/2 inch (6 to 13 mm) for jams and fruit. Remove air bubbles with a plastic tool, wipe the rims clean, and apply lids and bands fingertip tight. Set jars on a rack in the canner and cover them with at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water. Start timing only when the water reaches a full rolling boil, and keep it boiling the whole time. If processing time is under 10 minutes, sterilize the empty jars first. Add time at higher altitudes as the recipe directs, because water boils at a lower temperature up high.

steps.title: Pressure can low-acid foods
steps.body: Put the rack and the amount of water the manual specifies in the canner, load the jars, and lock the lid. Virginia Cooperative Extension stresses venting: let steam pour from the open vent for a full 10 minutes before adding the weight or closing the petcock. Skipping this leaves air inside, so the canner will not reach a safe temperature. Bring it to pressure, then start timing. Keep pressure at or above the target the whole time. If it drops below, bring it back up and restart the timing from zero. Turn off the heat at the end, and let the canner cool and depressurize on its own.

steps.title: Adjust pressure for your altitude
steps.body: Higher altitude means lower pressure from the air, so you add gauge pressure. Virginia Extension gives these targets for most tested recipes. Dial gauge: 11 pounds at 0 to 2,000 feet, 12 pounds at 2,001 to 4,000 feet, 13 pounds at 4,001 to 6,000 feet, 14 pounds at 6,001 to 8,000 feet, and 15 pounds at 8,001 to 10,000 feet. Weighted gauge: 10 pounds at 0 to 1,000 feet and 15 pounds above 1,000 feet. Have dial gauges tested every year at your extension office or by the maker. Replace a gauge that reads more than 2 pounds off. Always follow the exact times in the tested recipe.

steps.title: Cool, check seals, and store
steps.body: Never force-cool a pressure canner with cold water or open the vent early. Wait until it reads zero, then wait 10 more minutes before opening the lid. Set jars on a towel away from drafts and leave them alone for 12 to 24 hours. A sealed lid curves down and does not flex when pressed. If a lid did not seal, reprocess within 24 hours using a new lid and the full time, or refrigerate the jar and eat it within a few days. Remove bands, wipe jars, label with contents and date, and store in a cool, dark, dry place. Use within about a year for best quality.

steps.title: Inspect before eating and discard bad jars
steps.body: Before opening, look for bulging or leaking lids, cracks, and broken seals. When you open the jar, watch for spurting liquid, foam, mold, off colors, or bad smells. The CDC says to throw out the food if any of these appear, and never taste food to test it. If you do not know whether a jar was canned with tested, safe methods, do not eat it - CDC says to throw it out (see the disposal steps above). For low-acid foods that WERE pressure canned correctly, some agencies add boiling the food for 10 minutes before eating (plus 1 minute per 1,000 feet above 1,000 feet) as an extra safety margin; this is never a fix for a doubtful or under-processed jar.

warnings: Water-bath canning green beans, corn, meat, or any low-acid food can cause botulism, which can kill. Pressure can them or do not can them.
Do not use electric multicookers, Instant Pot-style appliances, ovens, or open kettles for canning.
Botulism toxin can be present with no sign of spoilage. Never taste questionable home-canned food.
Seek emergency care right away for double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, or weakness after eating home-canned food.
proTips: Write your elevation and the matching canner pressure on a card taped inside your canning recipe binder.
Print the NCHFP and USDA guides now. Canning is most valuable when the internet is gone.
Buy lids in bulk. Flat lids are single-use for canning; bands and jars can be reused if not nicked or rusted.
source: CDC / USDA / NCHFP / Virginia Cooperative Extension

sources.title: Since You Can't Have Too Many Tomatoes
sources.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation

sources.title: USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning - Guide 1: Principles of Home Canning
sources.publisher: USDA / National Center for Home Food Preservation

whenNotTo: No tested recipe exists for the food - freeze, dry, or eat it instead.
You cannot keep a steady heat source for the full processing time - pressure drops make low-acid food unsafe.
Your dial gauge has not been tested or reads more than 2 pounds off.

quickGlance.situation: You want to can garden produce or meat for long-term storage without refrigeration.
immediate: Pressure can vegetables, meat, beans, and fish; water-bath only high-acid or acidified foods.
Use a USDA or NCHFP tested recipe exactly as written.
Set canner pressure for your altitude and vent 10 minutes first.
then: Check seals after 12 to 24 hours and label jars with the date.
Discard any jar that bulges, leaks, spurts, or smells off - do not taste it.

title: Seed Saving - Open-Pollinated vs. Hybrid and Storage
summary: Save your own garden seed year after year: choose varieties that come true from seed, prevent cross-pollination, clean and dry seed correctly, and store it so it stays alive.

steps.title: Grow open-pollinated varieties
steps.body: UMass Extension says successful seed saving requires open-pollinated varieties rather than hybrids. Open-pollinated (OP) plants, including heirlooms, produce seed that grows into plants much like the parent. Hybrid seed, labeled F1, is made by crossing two different parent lines. Seed saved from a hybrid will not reliably match it. The next generation can vary in size, flavor, and vigor. Check seed packets and catalogs for the words open-pollinated or heirloom. If you are building a long-term garden for self-reliance, buy OP seed for your main crops now, while it is easy to get.

steps.title: Start with easy self-pollinating crops
steps.body: Some crops usually pollinate themselves inside a single flower, so they rarely cross with neighbors. UMass Extension names tomatoes, lettuce, beans, and peas as good first seed-saving crops for this reason. Saving their seed is simple and the results are reliable. Other crops cross easily by insects or wind. Squash and pumpkins cross freely within the same species. Brassicas such as kale, cabbage, broccoli, collards, and cauliflower cross with each other. Corn is wind-pollinated and crosses across long distances. Save those for later, once you have learned isolation methods.

steps.title: Prevent unwanted crosses
steps.body: To keep cross-pollinating crops true, grow only one variety of that species at a time, separate varieties by distance or timing, or cover the flowers and hand-pollinate. To hand-pollinate squash, tape shut a male and a female flower the evening before they open. The next morning, rub the male flower's pollen onto the female flower, then tape the female flower shut again and mark the stem. Seed from that fruit will be true. Remember that your neighbor's garden counts too. Bees travel, so a zucchini over the fence can cross with yours.

steps.title: Pick the best plants and let seed mature
steps.body: Save seed from several healthy plants with the traits you want, such as early fruit, good flavor, disease resistance, or drought tolerance. Saving from many plants keeps genetic variety. Never save from sick or weak plants. Let the seed mature fully. Beans and peas should dry in the pod on the plant until they rattle. Corn should dry on the stalk. Lettuce goes to seed after flowering and is ready when the fluffy seed heads appear. Squash and pumpkin fruit should be fully ripe, and UMass Extension notes that storing the fruit for a month or two afterward improves seed vigor.

steps.title: Clean wet and dry seeds the right way
steps.body: Dry seeds such as beans, peas, corn, and lettuce can be shelled or shaken out. Lettuce heads can be dried upside down in a paper bag, which catches the seed. Tomatoes are wet-processed. Scoop seeds and pulp into a jar with a little water and let it sit a few days, stirring daily. Pulp and dead seeds float and can be poured off. Good seeds sink. Rinse the good seed and spread it thin to dry. For squash and pumpkins, rinse the pulp away and discard flat, thin seeds, which will not grow.

steps.title: Dry seed thoroughly
steps.body: Moisture kills stored seed. Spread cleaned seed in a single layer on a plate, screen, or paper towel in a warm, airy spot out of direct sun. UMass Extension says tomato seed needs about two weeks and squash seed a few weeks. Stir it every day or two so it dries evenly. Seed is dry enough when large seeds snap or shatter rather than bend, and small seeds pour freely without clumping. Do not dry seed in an oven or in hot sun, which can kill the embryo.

steps.title: Store seed cool, dry, and dark
steps.body: Put dry seed in a sealed, opaque container such as a labeled envelope inside a glass jar or a metal tin. Store it somewhere cool and stable, like a dark closet or the refrigerator. Cold, dry conditions slow the seed's metabolism and help it live longer. Add a packet of silica gel or a spoon of dry rice wrapped in tissue to absorb moisture. Label each packet with the crop, variety, and year. Before the next season, do a germination test: roll 10 seeds in a damp paper towel, keep it warm, and count how many sprout. If fewer than about 7 sprout, plant more thickly or refresh your stock.

warnings: Seed saved from hybrid (F1) plants will not grow true. Do not rely on it for your next crop.
Seeds treated with fungicide (often dyed pink, blue, or green) are poisonous. Never eat them or feed them to animals.
Do not save seed from diseased plants. Some diseases pass through the seed.
proTips: Swap seed with neighbors and local seed libraries to keep a wide genetic base and varieties adapted to your area.
Keep a backup supply of purchased seed for each staple crop in case a saved batch fails.
Grow the seed crop in a separate corner and mark the plants so no one harvests them by mistake.
whenNotTo: The variety is a hybrid (F1) or a patented/licensed variety whose seed may not be saved or shared.
Your plants were diseased this season - buy clean seed instead.

quickGlance.situation: You want to grow next year's garden from seed you produce yourself.
immediate: Choose open-pollinated or heirloom varieties.
Start with beans, peas, tomatoes, and lettuce.
Save seed from several of your best, healthiest plants.
then: Dry seed fully, then store it sealed, cool, and dark.
Germination-test each batch before planting season.

title: Composting - Turning Waste Into Garden Soil
summary: Build a compost pile that heats up and breaks down fast, using the right mix of browns and greens, water, and air, and keep out materials that cause smells, pests, or disease.

steps.title: Pick a site and a bin
steps.body: Choose a level, well-drained spot that you can reach easily with a wheelbarrow and a hose, but away from your well and not draining into a stream. Partial shade keeps the pile from drying out. A bin is optional but keeps things neat. Simple options include a ring of welded wire fencing, a three-sided box of pallets, or a purchased tumbler. Two or three side-by-side bins let you fill one while another finishes. Check local rules, since some towns require covered bins.

steps.title: Balance browns and greens
steps.body: Compost needs carbon and nitrogen. Browns are dry, woody, carbon-rich materials such as fallen leaves, straw, shredded paper, and plain cardboard. Greens are moist, nitrogen-rich materials such as grass clippings, vegetable and fruit scraps, coffee grounds, and chicken manure with bedding. UConn Extension says decomposition is fastest at about 25 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen, which works out to roughly one-third greens and two-thirds browns by volume. Too many greens make a slimy, smelly pile. Too many browns make a pile that just sits. Chop or shred big pieces so microbes have more surface to work on.

steps.title: Build a pile big enough to heat
steps.body: Size matters. UConn Extension recommends a pile about 3 to 4 feet (1 to 1.2 m) high and wide for hot composting. Smaller piles lose heat and break down slowly. Build it in layers of browns and greens, or mix them as you go. Add a shovel of garden soil or finished compost to bring in microbes. Water each layer so the whole pile is evenly damp, about like a wrung-out sponge. A good hot pile should reach about 140°F (60°C) within a few days. A long compost thermometer lets you check the core.

steps.title: Turn and water the pile
steps.body: Microbes need air. Turn the pile at least once a month, moving the outside material into the center. In a hot pile, turn it whenever the core temperature drops to about 100°F (38°C), which restarts the heating. Check moisture each time. If it is dry and dusty inside, add water. If it is soggy and smells sour or like ammonia, mix in dry browns. In rainy climates, cover the pile with a tarp so it does not get waterlogged.

steps.title: Keep the wrong things out
steps.body: UConn Extension advises leaving out meat, bones, fats, oils, and dog or cat droppings. These attract rats, raccoons, and flies, and pet waste can carry parasites that infect people. Also skip dairy, diseased plants, weeds that have gone to seed, and plants treated with herbicides, because a cool home pile may not kill the problem. Avoid limestone and wood ash in large amounts, and never add coal ash, treated or painted wood, or glossy printed paper. Chicken, rabbit, goat, and cow manure with their bedding are excellent additions.

steps.title: Know when it is finished
steps.body: Depending on materials and how often you turn it, compost can be ready in about a month or take up to a year. It is finished when you can no longer recognize the original materials and it is dark, crumbly, and smells like earth. Let it cure for a few weeks after it stops heating so it is stable before you use it around seedlings. Screen out chunks through a 1/2 inch (13 mm) mesh and toss them back into a new pile.

steps.title: Use compost safely in the garden
steps.body: Spread 1 to 3 inches (2.5 to 7.5 cm) of finished compost over beds and work it into the top few inches of soil, or use it as a mulch around plants. Penn State Extension notes you can blend up to half finished compost into soilless mix for containers. If your compost includes animal manure, use fully finished compost, and avoid adding fresh or partly composted manure to beds of crops eaten raw close to harvest. Wash your hands after handling compost and manure, and wash garden produce before eating.

warnings: Never compost dog, cat, or human waste for food gardens. It can spread parasites and disease.
Raw or partly composted manure can carry E. coli and Salmonella. Do not put it on crops eaten raw near harvest time.
A very large, wet pile of fresh grass or hay can heat high enough to smolder. Keep piles a moderate size and turn them.
proTips: Keep a sealed bucket in the kitchen for scraps and a stockpile of dry leaves next to the bin to cover each addition.
Spent chicken litter is an ideal compost starter - it already mixes browns and greens.
Use compost tea or finished compost to stretch scarce fertilizer when you cannot buy any.

sources.title: Container Vegetable Gardening: Four Keys to Success

whenNotTo: You have only meat, fat, or pet waste to dispose of - bury or bag it instead.
The only site drains toward your well or a creek.

quickGlance.situation: You want free fertilizer and better soil from kitchen and yard waste.
immediate: Mix about two parts browns to one part greens.
Build a pile about 3 to 4 feet high and wide.
Keep it damp like a wrung-out sponge.
then: Turn it when the core cools or at least monthly.
Use it when it is dark, crumbly, and smells earthy.

title: Raising Rabbits for Meat
summary: Raise meat rabbits in a small space: housing, feed, breeding and kindling, heat protection, and sanitation, based on Oregon State and Alabama extension guidance.

steps.title: Check rules and start with a small trio
steps.body: Rabbits are quiet and fit in small yards, but check zoning, HOA, and lease rules before you buy. A common starter herd is one buck and two does of a medium or large meat breed, such as New Zealand White or Californian. Buy from a breeder who keeps records and healthy stock. Look for clear eyes, clean noses and ears, firm droppings, and no sores on the feet. Plan for processing as well as raising. You will need a humane, legal way to slaughter and a cold place to chill meat.

steps.title: House each adult separately
steps.body: Keep each adult rabbit in its own cage or hutch, because adults fight and unplanned breeding happens fast. Give each animal enough room to stretch out and stand up, with more space for large breeds and for does with litters. Hutches should be shaded, well ventilated, and sheltered from rain, wind, and predators. Alabama Extension notes that fresh air cuts disease and offsets the ammonia from urine. Clean droppings out from under cages often. Wire floors should have a solid resting board so rabbits can get off the wire, which helps prevent sore hocks.

steps.title: Feed a balanced ration and clean water
steps.body: Oregon State Extension advises 3 to 9 ounces (85 to 255 g) of feed per rabbit per day depending on size and stage. Pregnant, nursing, and growing rabbits need the most. For meat breeds, pellets with 16 to 18 percent protein give the fastest growth. Offer grass hay such as timothy, and use alfalfa hay to boost protein if pellets are lower in it. Keep treats like carrots small and rare. Rabbits need clean, fresh water at all times, and they drink much more in heat. Store feed sealed, cool, and dry, since moldy feed can kill rabbits.

steps.title: Breed at the right age and track dates
steps.body: Oregon State Extension gives sexual maturity at about 4 to 6 months for small breeds, 7 to 9 months for medium breeds, and 9 to 11 months for large breeds. Always take the doe to the buck's cage, not the other way around, to reduce fighting. Write down the breeding date. Gestation runs 28 to 35 days, averaging 31. You can learn to feel for kits by palpation after about 10 days. Give the doe a nest box with clean, dry bedding a few days before her due date. She will pull fur to line it.

steps.title: Care for kits through weaning
steps.body: Check the litter once soon after birth and remove any dead kits, then leave the nest alone for a few days so the doe does not abandon it. Kits born on bare wire can die, so make sure the doe kindles in the box. Oregon State Extension suggests removing the nest box at about 2 to 3 weeks and weaning at about 2 months. Separate young bucks and does before they start breeding. Most growers raise fryers to a few pounds and process them at a young age while the meat is tender.

steps.title: Protect rabbits from heat
steps.body: Heat is a major killer. Alabama Extension says rabbits do best at about 50 to 60°F (10 to 16°C) and cope poorly above 90°F (32°C), especially with high humidity. Heat can make bucks temporarily sterile and cause does to abort or abandon litters. Keep hutches shaded, hang fans to move air over (not straight at) the cages, and put frozen water bottles in cages for rabbits to lean against. Keep the rabbits dry if you use misters. Many raisers stop breeding in midsummer and breed in fall, winter, and spring.

steps.title: Keep it clean and handle meat safely
steps.body: Sanitation is essential. Dirty cages lead to disease and poor growth. Remove manure regularly and compost it, since rabbit manure is an excellent garden fertilizer. Disinfect cages between litters. Trim nails up to, but not past, the pink quick. Watch for runny noses, crusty ears, diarrhea, and sore feet, and isolate sick animals. When processing, wear gloves, keep meat cold, and cook rabbit to at least 160°F (71°C). Wild rabbits can carry tularemia, so never handle a wild rabbit that acts sick or was found dead.

warnings: Rabbits die quickly from heat stress. Provide shade, airflow, and water every hot day.
Keep adults in separate cages. Rabbits can injure or kill each other and breed constantly if housed together.
Moldy or spoiled feed can kill rabbits. Store feed sealed and dry.
Wear gloves when dressing rabbits and do not handle wild rabbits that seem sick.
proTips: Rabbit manure can go straight onto garden beds without burning plants, and it makes great compost.
Keep a simple record card on each cage with breeding dates, litter sizes, and weaning weights so you keep the best breeders.
Freeze empty plastic bottles every night in summer. It is the cheapest rabbit cooling system there is.
whenNotTo: You cannot provide shade and cooling in a hot climate.
Local rules forbid livestock or slaughter on your property.

quickGlance.situation: You want a steady, quiet source of meat that fits in a small backyard.
immediate: Start with one buck and two does of a meat breed.
House each adult in its own shaded, ventilated cage.
Feed 16 to 18 percent protein pellets, hay, and constant clean water.
then: Record breeding dates and add a nest box before kindling.
Cool rabbits in summer and keep cages clean.

title: Dairy and Meat Goats - The Basics
summary: Start a small goat herd for milk or meat: choosing breeds and healthy stock, fencing and shelter, feeding, vaccination and parasites, and clean milking, based on extension guidance.

steps.title: Decide on milk, meat, or both
steps.body: Dairy breeds include Nubian, Alpine, Saanen, Toggenburg, LaMancha, and the small Nigerian Dwarf, which gives less milk but very high butterfat. Oregon State Extension notes a normal lactation lasts about 305 days. Meat breeds include Boer, Kiko, and Spanish goats, covered in Oklahoma State's meat goat manual. Goats are herd animals and are stressed when kept alone, so plan on at least two. Check zoning before you buy. Many towns limit goats or allow only small breeds. Bucks smell strong and need separate, sturdier housing, so many small keepers own only does and borrow a buck or use a breeding service.

steps.title: Buy healthy, tested animals
steps.body: Disease you bring home is very hard to get rid of. Oregon State and UF/IFAS Extension advise buying only from herds tested free of CAE (caprine arthritis encephalitis), which has no treatment, and checking for CL (caseous lymphadenitis), which causes abscesses. Ask for test records and look at the animals in person. Healthy goats are alert, with bright eyes, clean noses, firm pellet droppings, and no lumps along the jaw or neck. Quarantine any new goat for at least 30 days before it joins your herd. Ask a local livestock veterinarian to look at them and help set up a health plan.

steps.title: Fence well and provide dry shelter
steps.body: Goats climb, jump, and test fences constantly. UF/IFAS Extension recommends a dog- and coyote-proof woven wire fence. Many keepers add a strand of electric wire to stop climbing and leaning. Goats hate getting wet, so give them a dry, well-ventilated shelter that keeps out rain and wind, plus shade in summer and constant access to fresh water. Keep the shelter floor dry with clean bedding. Remove toxic plants from pens, including ornamental shrubs such as azalea, rhododendron, yew, and cherry laurel.

steps.title: Feed mostly forage, plus minerals
steps.body: Goats are ruminants and do best on roughage: browse, pasture, and good grass or alfalfa-mix hay. UF/IFAS Extension says concentrates (grain) should supplement energy and protein. Aim for 16 to 18 percent crude protein grain with grass hay, or 14 to 16 percent with legume hay like alfalfa. A rule of thumb for milkers is about 1 pound of grain for every 3 pounds of milk in mid-lactation. Provide a loose mineral made for goats. Sheep minerals are often low in copper for goats. Make feed changes slowly, since sudden grain overloads can cause deadly bloat.

steps.title: Vaccinate and manage parasites
steps.body: The common core vaccine is CDT, which protects against two types of Clostridium perfringens (enterotoxemia) and tetanus. UF/IFAS Extension says does usually get a booster 4 to 6 weeks before kidding, and kids get a series in their first months. Your vet sets the schedule. Internal worms, especially the barber pole worm, are the top goat health problem in warm, wet areas. Have fecal samples tested, deworm only animals that need it and only per label or vet direction, feed from feeders rather than the ground, and rotate pastures. Overusing dewormers breeds resistant worms.

steps.title: Milk cleanly and handle milk safely
steps.body: Milk on a clean stand, twice a day, at the same times. Clean and dry the teats before milking and dip them in a teat disinfectant after. Oregon State Extension recommends regular mastitis checks, such as the California Mastitis Test, and dumping milk from any goat given antibiotics or other drugs for the withdrawal time on the label. Strain milk and chill it quickly, ideally below 40°F (4°C). Pasteurizing kills disease-causing germs. Raw milk can carry bacteria that are especially dangerous to children, pregnant women, older adults, and people with weak immune systems, so pasteurize before drinking whenever you can.

steps.title: Plan for kidding and routine care
steps.body: Does usually have 1 to 3 kids a year. Learn the signs of labor, normal birth positions, and when to call a vet before the first kidding. Make sure newborn kids nurse colostrum within the first hours. UF/IFAS Extension suggests kids begin nibbling hay and grain at 1 to 2 weeks and can be weaned once they eat at least 1/4 pound (115 g) of grain daily. Trim hooves at least once a year, and more often on soft ground. Check each goat daily for appetite, droppings, and behavior. A goat that stops eating needs attention the same day.

warnings: Raw milk can spread serious infections. Pasteurize it, especially for children, pregnant women, and older adults.
Never bring untested goats into your herd. CAE and CL spread and are hard or impossible to clear.
Sudden access to large amounts of grain can cause fatal bloat or enterotoxemia. Lock up feed bins.
Bucks can be aggressive, especially during breeding season. Never turn your back on one.
proTips: Two Nigerian Dwarf does fit a small yard and can supply a family with milk for drinking and cheese.
Learn FAMACHA eye-color scoring at a local extension workshop to spot anemia from barber pole worms early.
Keep a herd notebook: vaccination dates, deworming, breeding, kidding, and milk weights.
source: UF/IFAS / Oregon State / Oklahoma State Extension

sources.title: What's Involved in Caring for Dairy Goats (4H427)

whenNotTo: You can keep only one goat - a lone goat is stressed and noisy.
You cannot milk twice a day, every day, while a doe is in milk.
You have no access to a livestock veterinarian for emergencies and kidding problems.

quickGlance.situation: You want a renewable supply of milk or meat from a small herd of goats.
immediate: Buy at least two goats from a CAE- and CL-tested herd.
Build woven-wire fencing and a dry, ventilated shelter.
Feed mostly hay and browse with goat minerals.
then: Set up CDT vaccination and fecal testing with a vet.
Milk cleanly, chill fast, and pasteurize.

title: Beekeeping Basics
summary: Start keeping honey bees for honey, wax, and better garden pollination: siting hives, safety gear, regular inspections, and the varroa mite monitoring that keeps colonies alive.

steps.title: Check laws, neighbors, and allergies
steps.body: Many states require you to register hives with the state apiary inspector, and some towns limit hive numbers or placement. Check before you buy. Talk to neighbors and ask to be told about outdoor events. Find out whether anyone in your household is allergic to stings. The Honey Bee Health Coalition notes that about 5 percent of people are allergic to bee venom. Anyone with a known severe allergy should see a doctor before working bees, and you should keep an epinephrine auto-injector on hand if one has been prescribed. Join a local beekeeping club. A mentor is the fastest way to learn.

steps.title: Get basic equipment
steps.body: Most beginners use a Langstroth hive: a bottom board, deep boxes for the brood nest, shallow or medium boxes called supers for honey, frames with foundation, an inner cover, and an outer cover. Screened bottom boards and a hive stand keep the hive off damp ground. You also need a hive tool to pry frames, a smoker, and protective gear. Always wear a veil, clothing that covers all skin, boots, and snug gloves. Buy bees as a package or a nucleus colony (nuc) from a reputable local supplier in spring. Starting with two hives lets you compare them and share frames if one struggles.

steps.title: Site the hives carefully
steps.body: Put hives where they get morning sun and some afternoon shade, with protection from strong wind. Give them clean water nearby, such as a shallow tray with stones to land on, so bees do not crowd your neighbor's pool or birdbath. Leave about 4 feet (1.2 m) of clear, level space around each hive for working. Face entrances away from paths and doors, or put a fence or hedge in front so bees fly up and over people. Bees forage up to about 2.5 miles (4 km), so an area with flowering plants through the season supports them best. In bear country, an electric fence is a must.

steps.title: Inspect calmly and regularly
steps.body: Inspect every 1 to 2 weeks in spring and summer on warm, calm days, usually midday when many foragers are out. Light the smoker with dry fuel and puff a little smoke at the entrance and under the cover. Work slowly and keep your body out of the flight path. Look for eggs and young larvae, which show the queen is laying, plus capped brood in a solid pattern, stored pollen and honey, and room to grow. Watch for queen cells, which mean the colony may swarm. Check for signs of disease such as sunken, greasy, or perforated brood caps, and get suspected American foulbrood confirmed by your state inspector.

steps.title: Monitor varroa mites
steps.body: Varroa mites are the leading cause of colony loss. The Honey Bee Health Coalition says looking at bees is not enough. Sample about 300 adult bees (roughly 1/2 cup) from a brood frame using an alcohol wash or a powdered sugar roll, and count the mites. Do this at least four times a year, starting in spring, but not when it is below 50°F (10°C). Divide the mites by 3 to get mites per 100 bees. In most seasons, 2 to 3 mites per 100 bees is the danger level to act on. Mite numbers can double in about a month, so check again after any treatment.

steps.title: Treat mites only with registered products
steps.body: When counts pass the threshold, treat all colonies in the same apiary at the same time. Use only EPA-registered mite treatments, follow every label instruction, and never use off-label or homemade chemicals. Rotate between treatment types so mites do not become resistant. The Coalition notes that older products such as Apistan and CheckMite+ often fail in North America because of resistance. Many treatments cannot be used while honey supers are on the hive, so plan timing around your honey harvest. Keep records of counts and treatments.

steps.title: Harvest honey and prepare for winter
steps.body: Take honey only from supers above the brood nest, and only frames that are mostly capped, which means the honey is ripe and will not ferment. Leave the colony enough honey to survive winter. In cold climates, that is often a full deep box or more. Feed sugar syrup in fall if stores are light. Reduce the entrance to help guard against robbing and mice. Replace old, dark brood comb gradually, about a few frames each year, so no brood frame is older than about five years. Do not give honey to babies under 1 year old, since it can cause infant botulism.

warnings: A sting can cause a life-threatening allergic reaction. If someone has trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or dizziness after a sting, use their epinephrine auto-injector and call 911.
Never give honey to infants under 12 months. It can cause infant botulism.
Use only EPA-registered mite treatments as labeled. Off-label chemicals can poison bees, honey, and you.
Never leave a lit smoker on dry grass or near the hive's wood. Smokers start fires.
proTips: Remove stingers quickly by scraping them out with a fingernail or hive tool.
Paint hives different colors and face them different ways to reduce bees drifting between colonies.
Keep a notebook and phone photos of each inspection. Records help you spot problems early.
source: Honey Bee Health Coalition (via CT Agricultural Experiment Station)

sources.title: Best Management Practices for Hive Health
sources.publisher: Honey Bee Health Coalition (hosted by Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station)

whenNotTo: Someone in the household has a severe bee venom allergy and no doctor's plan.
Local rules ban hives, or the only site is right next to a neighbor's door or a busy path.

quickGlance.situation: You want honey, wax, and better pollination from your own hives.
immediate: Check state registration rules and household sting allergies.
Buy gear, a veil, and a nuc or package from a local supplier.
Site hives with morning sun, water, and a flight barrier.
then: Inspect every 1 to 2 weeks in season.
Count varroa mites at least four times a year and act at 2 to 3 per 100 bees.

title: Root Cellars and Cold Storage Without Refrigeration
summary: Keep potatoes, roots, cabbage, squash, onions, and apples for months with no power by matching each crop to the right temperature and humidity in a cellar, basement, pit, or buried container.

steps.title: Sort crops by the conditions they need
steps.body: Stored produce is still alive and breathing, so each crop wants different conditions. UConn Extension groups them roughly like this. Potatoes, carrots, beets, turnips, parsnips, and other roots want cold and very humid air, about 90 to 95 percent humidity, just above freezing. Apples also like cold and moist. Pumpkins and winter squash want warmer, drier air at about 60 to 75 percent humidity. Onions and garlic want cool and dry. Plan your storage spaces around these groups instead of putting everything in one room, where some crops will rot and others will shrivel.

steps.title: Harvest and cure before storing
steps.body: Only perfect produce stores well. Handle crops gently, and set aside anything bruised, cut, or diseased to eat first. Many crops need curing before storage. Potatoes are commonly cured for about two weeks in a dark, humid spot around 50 to 60°F (10 to 16°C) to heal skin nicks. Winter squash and pumpkins (except acorn types) are commonly cured for about 10 days in warm conditions to harden the rind. Onions and garlic are dried in an airy, shaded spot until the necks are tight and the skins papery. Do not wash root crops before storing; brush off loose soil and cut tops to about 1 inch (2.5 cm).

steps.title: Use the spaces you already have
steps.body: You may not need to dig a cellar. UConn Extension lists several options. An unheated basement corner, especially a north-side corner walled off with insulation and a vent, can hold roots and apples. A heated basement around 50 to 60°F (10 to 16°C) works short-term for squash, sweet potatoes, potatoes, and onions. An unheated room, attic, or pantry can hold potatoes and onions if it does not freeze. A garage, shed, or breezeway can work if it does not hold fuel, chemicals, or vehicles, which can taint flavor.

steps.title: Build simple pits, mounds, and buried cans
steps.body: Roots and cabbage can be stored outdoors. Pick a well-drained site, lay down straw, stack the crop, cover it with more straw, hay, or dry leaves, and then add soil to insulate. A buried 20-gallon (76-liter) metal or plastic trash can with a few small drainage holes, sunk so the rim sits a few inches above ground and covered with a lid and a thick layer of straw, keeps rodents out. Carrots, beets, turnips, rutabagas, winter radishes, kohlrabi, celery root, and cabbage do well this way. UConn Extension notes that once you open a pit, use the contents within 1 to 2 weeks.

steps.title: Control temperature, humidity, and air
steps.body: Aim for steady temperatures between just above freezing and about 40°F (4°C) for most roots and apples, with little swing from day to night. Use vents or a window you can open on cold nights and close on warm days. Put a cheap thermometer and humidity gauge in each space. To raise humidity for roots, pack them in damp sand, sawdust, or peat in boxes, or put pans of water or wet burlap on the floor. A dirt floor helps. For onions and squash, keep the air dry and moving.

steps.title: Keep apples and pears away from vegetables
steps.body: Fruits give off ethylene gas as they ripen. UConn Extension warns that ethylene speeds ripening and spoilage of nearby vegetables. It can make potatoes sprout and carrots turn bitter. Store apples and pears in a separate room, or at least well away from vegetables and wrapped individually in paper. Strong-smelling crops such as onions, cabbage, and rutabagas can also pass their odor to other produce, so give them their own space or cover.

steps.title: Check weekly and protect from pests
steps.body: One rotting potato can spoil a bin. UConn Extension advises checking stored produce at least weekly for rot, mold, moisture, and rodents. Remove anything soft, moldy, or sprouting, and use it or compost it. Throw out moldy soft produce. Seal gaps against mice with metal, plastic, or mesh with openings under 1/4 inch (6 mm). Use clean, food-grade bins, and do not use insulation that could contaminate food. At the end of the season, empty and clean every container and the room. Potatoes that turn green have a natural toxin. Cut away green parts and discard any very green potatoes.

warnings: Do not store produce near gasoline, solvents, pesticides, or vehicle exhaust. Fumes taint food and can be toxic.
Green potatoes contain solanine. Cut away green areas and discard heavily green or bitter potatoes.
A walk-in cellar can collect carbon dioxide or radon in some areas. Ventilate it, and test basements for radon.
Freezing ruins most stored crops. Watch the thermometer during hard cold snaps.
proTips: Leave carrots and parsnips in the ground under a thick straw mulch in well-drained soil and dig them as needed.
Store the best keepers on purpose: late cabbage, storage onions, russet potatoes, and butternut squash outlast early varieties.
Label each bin with the crop and date, and eat the shortest-keeping crops first.

sources.title: Cold Storage: A Sustainable Way to Preserve the Harvest

whenNotTo: Your climate is too warm in fall and winter to hold produce below about 50°F - dry or can instead.
The crop is damaged or already rotting - eat or preserve it now.
The storage site floods or drains poorly.

quickGlance.situation: You have a fall harvest to keep for months without a refrigerator.
immediate: Sort crops into cold-moist, cool-dry, and warm-dry groups.
Cure potatoes, squash, and onions before storing.
Keep apples away from vegetables.
then: Watch temperature and humidity in each space.
Check weekly and remove anything rotting.

title: Drying, Smoking, and Curing Meat Safely
summary: Make jerky, smoked meat, and home-cured pork that will not make you sick, using USDA FSIS jerky temperatures and extension-tested curing and smoking guidance.

steps.title: Start with cold, clean meat
steps.body: Every safe preserved meat starts with fresh meat kept at 40°F (4°C) or colder. USDA FSIS advises washing hands and equipment before and after handling raw meat, thawing frozen meat in the refrigerator rather than on the counter, and using or freezing ground meat and poultry within 2 days and whole cuts of red meat within 3 to 5 days. Game needs extra care. FSIS warns that venison can be heavily contaminated with fecal bacteria depending on how the animal was shot and dressed, and deer carcasses often sit warm for hours. Trim away bloodshot or soiled meat. Partly freezing meat makes it easier to slice thin and evenly.

steps.title: Heat jerky to 160°F before or during drying
steps.body: This is the key update many old recipes miss. USDA FSIS says to heat meat to 160°F (71°C), and poultry to 165°F (74°C), before drying, because a dehydrator alone may not kill bacteria such as Salmonella and E. coli. Marinate in the refrigerator and do not reuse the marinade. Then steam or roast the strips until a food thermometer reads 160°F in the thickest strips. Slice meat about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick or less so it heats and dries evenly. Ground meat jerky carries more risk because bacteria are mixed throughout, so heating is even more important.

steps.title: Dry at a steady 130 to 140°F and store briefly
steps.body: After heating, dry the strips in a dehydrator or oven that holds a steady 130 to 140°F (54 to 60°C) the whole time. A dehydrator with an adjustable thermostat makes this much easier. Dry until a cooled piece cracks when bent but does not snap. Pat off beads of fat, which go rancid. Cool, then pack in clean, airtight containers. FSIS says home-dried jerky keeps about 1 to 2 months at room temperature. Commercial jerky lasts longer because it is made under controlled conditions. Freeze extra for longer storage.

steps.title: Cure only with a measured commercial cure
steps.body: Mississippi State Extension recommends a prepackaged commercial cure that contains sodium nitrite, used exactly at the rate printed on that product's label or in a tested recipe written for that exact product. Cure products differ greatly in strength: pink curing salt (often called Prague Powder #1, about 6.25% sodium nitrite) is used in very small amounts - typically about 1 level teaspoon per 5 pounds of meat - while some ready-mixed cures are mostly salt and are used by the ounce. Never swap one cure for another or reuse a rate from a different product or recipe; using a strong cure at a weak cure's rate can cause nitrite poisoning. Weigh or measure precisely. Nitrite helps protect cured meat against botulism, but too much is toxic. Never use more than the label or recipe says, and keep curing salts clearly labeled, away from table salt and children. Use only meat in good condition and keep it at 32 to 40°F (0 to 4°C) the entire time it cures. Warm curing lets spoilage and dangerous bacteria grow before the salt penetrates.

steps.title: Give the cure enough time
steps.body: Salt moves slowly. For dry-cured hams and shoulders, Mississippi State Extension gives about 7 days per inch (2.5 cm) of thickness at the thickest point, so a 5-inch ham needs about 35 days. Rub the cure on in two to four applications, 3 to 5 days apart, depending on the cut. Short cures of 2 to 3 weeks make milder meat that is not fully cured and must be frozen or refrigerated. Bacon is cured for a shorter time and is meant to be cooked. Write the start date and planned finish date on a tag on each piece.

steps.title: Smoke at safe temperatures and cook fully
steps.body: Hot smoking cooks as it smokes. Mississippi State Extension describes drying at about 125°F (52°C) with no smoke, smoking at about 135°F (57°C), then finishing at about 180°F (82°C) until the ham's center reaches 142°F (61°C). Hams taken only to 142°F still need full cooking at home before eating. Cold smoking, under 100°F (38°C) and ideally 70 to 80°F (21 to 27°C), adds flavor but does not cook or make meat safe. Use it only on fully cured meat, and cook the meat afterward unless you are following a tested dry-cure recipe. Spoilage bacteria grow fastest between about 80 and 110°F (27 and 43°C).

steps.title: Store cured meat correctly
steps.body: Anything that is not fully dry-cured and aged must be wrapped airtight and frozen quickly after smoking and cooling. Long room-temperature aging of country hams takes months at controlled temperature and humidity. Mississippi State Extension does not promote home aging in warm, humid climates because the product may not be safe. Beginners should freeze or refrigerate all cured meat, cook it before eating, and treat dry-aged, uncooked products like salami and prosciutto as projects for later, after hands-on training. Wild game such as bear and wild boar can carry Trichinella parasites, so cook those meats thoroughly rather than relying on curing or drying.

warnings: Old jerky recipes that skip the 160°F heating step can cause Salmonella and E. coli illness. Heat meat to 160°F (poultry 165°F) first.
Curing salts with nitrite are poisonous in excess. Measure exactly and store them labeled and out of reach.
