Cold-smoked meat is not cooked. Cook it fully unless it is a tested, fully dry-cured product.
Curing does not reliably kill parasites in bear, wild boar, or other wild game. Cook those meats thoroughly.
Get emergency care for vomiting with severe diarrhea, high fever, or any vision, speech, or swallowing problems after eating preserved meat.
proTips: Do curing in late fall and winter, when an unheated garage or cellar holds 32 to 40°F without a refrigerator.
A cheap probe thermometer is the single most important food safety tool for jerky and smoking.
Cut a test strip from the thickest part of the batch to check heating and dryness.
source: USDA FSIS / Mississippi State Extension / NCHFP

sources.title: Cure and Smoke Review: Meats
sources.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation

whenNotTo: You cannot keep curing meat at 32 to 40°F - freeze the meat instead and cure it later.
You have no thermometer to confirm 160°F for jerky.
The meat was left warm, smells off, or came from a sick animal.

quickGlance.situation: You have meat to preserve without a freezer and want to dry, smoke, or cure it safely.
immediate: Keep raw meat at 40°F or colder until you start.
For jerky, heat strips to 160°F (poultry 165°F), then dry at 130 to 140°F.
Cure only with a measured commercial nitrite cure at 32 to 40°F.
then: Store home jerky 1 to 2 months; freeze cured meat that is not fully dry-cured.
Cook cured and cold-smoked meat fully before eating.

title: Small-Space and Container Gardening for Apartments and Suburbs
summary: Grow real food on a balcony, patio, rooftop, or small yard using containers: pot sizes, potting mix, sun, watering, feeding, and the best compact crops, based on Penn State Extension guidance.

steps.title: Map your sun and check the rules
steps.body: Watch your space for a full day and note how many hours of direct sun each spot gets. Penn State Extension says tomatoes and peppers need at least 6 hours of sun a day. Lettuce, kale, and other greens can handle some shade, and most herbs fall in between. South- and west-facing balconies are usually best. Before you start, check your lease, HOA, or building rules on balcony loads, hanging planters, and water runoff. Wet soil is heavy, so keep large containers near walls and railings where structures are strongest, and never block fire exits.

steps.title: Choose containers big enough
steps.body: Bigger pots hold more water and roots, so plants stress less. Penn State Extension recommends a container at least 20 inches (50 cm) wide for a tomato, about 14 inches (35 cm) wide for a pepper or eggplant, and smaller pots for herbs and greens. Pots should be at least as deep as they are wide. Every container needs drainage holes. Plastic pots are light and dry out slowly. Terracotta dries faster. Heavy cement or stone pots keep tall plants from tipping in wind. Fabric grow bags, 5-gallon (19-liter) buckets with holes drilled in the bottom, and food-grade totes all work. Avoid containers that held chemicals.

steps.title: Fill with potting mix, not garden soil
steps.body: Penn State Extension advises a soilless potting mix rather than garden soil, which packs down in pots and drains poorly. You can blend in up to about half finished compost to add nutrients and hold moisture. Fill containers to about 1 inch (2.5 cm) below the rim so water does not spill over. Refresh or replace mix each season, or at least mix in new compost, since old mix compacts and can carry disease. Raise pots slightly on feet or blocks so water can drain freely and does not stain balconies.

steps.title: Pick compact, productive crops
steps.body: Choose dwarf, bush, patio, or determinate varieties bred for containers. Good choices include cherry and determinate tomatoes, peppers, bush beans, lettuce and other salad greens, kale, Swiss chard, green onions, radishes, and herbs like basil, parsley, and chives. Pole beans, cucumbers, and vining tomatoes still work if you give them a trellis. Penn State suggests leaving sweet corn, watermelon, winter squash, and zucchini for in-ground gardens because they need so much space. Potatoes can grow in deep bags or bins, adding mix as they grow.

steps.title: Water often and deeply
steps.body: Containers dry out much faster than garden beds. Penn State Extension says to water at least once a day in hot summer weather, and twice for small pots or very hot, windy balconies. Water until it runs out the bottom so the whole root zone is wet. Check by pushing a finger an inch into the mix. If it is dry, water. If it is still moist, wait. Keep mix moist but never soggy. Saucers can help in heat but should not stay full of standing water, which rots roots and breeds mosquitoes. Self-watering containers and drip lines on a timer save time.

steps.title: Feed regularly
steps.body: Frequent watering washes nutrients out of pots, so container plants need steady feeding. Penn State Extension recommends mixing slow-release fertilizer into the potting mix at planting, then giving a soluble fertilizer every 2 to 4 weeks. Follow the label rate. More is not better and can burn roots. Compost, worm castings, and rabbit or aged chicken manure compost are good low-cost boosters. Yellowing lower leaves often mean the plant needs nitrogen. Pale, slow growth in cool weather may just be the temperature.

steps.title: Stretch space and seasons
steps.body: Grow up instead of out with trellises, railing planters, and hanging baskets for herbs and strawberries. Replant each pot as soon as a crop finishes: start with spring lettuce, follow with summer peppers, and end with fall greens. Move pots to chase sun or to shelter them from early frosts and summer heat. Indoors, a sunny south window or an inexpensive LED grow light can produce greens and herbs all winter. Keep a list of what grows best in your space and replant those first.

warnings: Wet soil is heavy. Large containers on balconies and rooftops can exceed load limits - check with your landlord or building manager.
Do not use containers that held chemicals, or old treated or painted wood, for food plants.
Secure tall plants and hanging pots so wind cannot throw them off balconies onto people below.
proTips: Group pots together. They shade each other's sides and hold moisture better.
A cut-and-come-again salad pot can give greens every week for months from one sowing.
Save 5-gallon food-grade buckets from bakeries and restaurants - drill drainage holes and they make free planters.

sources.title: Container Vegetable Gardening: Four Keys to Success

whenNotTo: Your space gets under about 3 hours of direct sun - stick to herbs and greens or use grow lights.
Your balcony or roof cannot safely carry the weight of wet containers.

quickGlance.situation: You have no yard, or only a small one, and want to grow some of your own food.
immediate: Find the spots with at least 6 hours of sun.
Get containers with drainage holes: 20 inches for tomatoes, 14 for peppers.
Fill with soilless potting mix, not garden soil.
then: Water daily in summer until it drains out the bottom.
Feed with soluble fertilizer every 2 to 4 weeks.
